claim_reasons: Terminated by Executive Order 12553, signed February 25, 1986, which orders that the listed Executive Orders, and any amendments thereto, are revoked, with no stated delayed effective date and no saving clause; the effective date is therefore the signing date, 1986-02-25. The table of revoked orders in the held text of Executive Order 12553 lists number 10010 with the subject "Creating an emergency board to investigate railroad labor disputes". This order created a board of three members to investigate the dispute between the Akron & Barberton Belt Railroad Company and other carriers named in List A and employees represented by the sixteen railway labor organizations named in List B, barred interested members, required a report within thirty days of October 18, 1948 (due by November 17, 1948), and froze changes in conditions from that date until thirty days after the report. Under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 on report deadlines, the report deadline and the end of the standstill are spent facts, functionally spent after the board reported and the standstill ran, and they are not the end; the order remained on the books until this express revocation. Executive Order 10015 (signed November 1948, effective as of October 18, 1948) amended this order by adding six carriers to List A and renaming two List B organizations. It is an amendment, not an end, because it left the order in force; it is not recorded as a later event on this clause because the only record of it in this order's dossier cites a transcription while an official Federal Register copy is held, and the policy requires the official copy. Executive Order 10015 has its own claim in this packet and ends on the same date.
rows.review_note: Reasoning expressly describes amendments/later events while the matching clause later_events is empty. This exactly supports the source-backed-event omission warning; it does not independently settle every event legal effect or whole lifecycle.

claim_reasons: Terminated by statute on June 14, 1935. The sole operative command approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Wine Industry under title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act ('do hereby approve said Code of Fair Competition for the Wine Industry.'); the introductory recital and the five numbered findings command nothing. Actor: Congress, S.J. Res. 113, section 2, approved June 14, 1935. Legal basis for the first end. An approval of a code under section 3 of title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act had legal effect only through section 3: under 3(b) the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry and a violation in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce was an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and district attorneys were directed to sue, and under 3(f) each violation was a misdemeanor (the section 3 excerpt held in this packet). Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935 (49 Stat. 375), repealed 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes' and states no effective date other than its approval. That repeal removed the power the approval rested on and every provision through which the approved code was enforced, which is the reason (not a default date) that it ends the prospective operative effect of this command on June 14, 1935. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495 (decided May 27, 1935), held the section 3 code-making delegation unconstitutional ('we hold the code provisions here in question to be invalid'); the held excerpts record that as a validity characterization (an approval under an unconstitutional delegation was void from issuance under the doctrine then prevailing, and May 27, 1935 is when that was declared), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no other approving order and a later doctrine treats a measure's earlier existence as an operative fact. June 16, 1935 is not an end: section 1 of the resolution replaced the two-year expiry in section 2(c) with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2. No held record shows this code cancelled or suspended before June 14, 1935; EO 6900 and EO 7020 amend the code and are later events, not ends.

Whereas the Federal Alcohol Control Administration has submitted for my approval amendments to the Code of Fair Competition for the Wine Industry and has rendered its report and recommendations and findings thereon; and

Whereas due notice of public hearing on said proposed amendments has been given and a public hearing thereon has been held pursuant to such notice;

Now, Therefore, by virtue of and pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 16, 1933 (ch. 90, 48 Stat. 195), and in order to effectuate the purposes of said Title, I hereby approve said amendments and modify my previous approval of the Code of Fair Competition for the Wine Industry to include an approval of said Code in its entirety as hereby amended.

FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT

The White House,

April 19, 1935.
